description: Architect a system of systems: classify the SoS type, identify constituent systems, define interfaces, analyze emergent behavior, and plan capability evolution.

steps.description: Classify the system of systems by governance model (directed, acknowledged, collaborative, virtual) and characterize constituent system independence, evolution authority, and operational autonomy.

inputs.name: mission-objectives
inputs.desc: The operational capabilities the SoS must deliver

inputs.name: constituent-system-list
inputs.desc: Known or candidate constituent systems and their current owners/operators

outputs.name: sos-classification
outputs.desc: Directed, acknowledged, collaborative, or virtual with justification

outputs.name: constituent-profiles
outputs.desc: Per-system profile: owner, operational independence level, evolution authority, interface maturity

process: List each constituent system and its current owner, operator, and funding source. A system with a single controlling authority points toward directed SoS; independent evolution authority points toward acknowledged or collaborative.

Score each constituent on three axes: operational independence (runs without the SoS), managerial independence (evolves on its own schedule), and geographic distribution. Sum the scores to place the SoS on the directed-to-virtual spectrum.
For each constituent, assess interface maturity on a 1-5 scale: 1 = no interface exists, 2 = ad hoc, 3 = documented but not controlled, 4 = controlled ICD, 5 = verified and regression-tested.
Document the classification with rationale. If the SoS spans multiple governance models (common in practice), identify which subgraph is directed and which is collaborative.

steps.description: Define and document interfaces between constituent systems at the physical, logical, and data layers using ICD best practice.

inputs.name: constituent-profiles
inputs.desc: Per-system profile with interface maturity scores

inputs.name: sos-classification
inputs.desc: SoS governance type

outputs.name: interface-catalog
outputs.desc: Complete catalog of inter-system interfaces with physical, logical, and data layer specifications

outputs.name: icd-gap-list
outputs.desc: Interfaces that lack formal documentation or verification, ranked by criticality

process: Build an N x N interaction matrix where rows and columns are constituent systems. For each cell, identify data exchanged, protocol, physical medium, and timing constraints.

For each interface, document three layers: physical (connector, cable, frequency band, voltage), logical (protocol, message format, handshake, error handling), and data (schema, units, valid ranges, update rate).
Assign each interface a criticality score: high if a failure breaks a mission capability, medium if it degrades performance, low if workarounds exist.
Flag interfaces where maturity is below 4 and criticality is high. These are the ICD gaps that drive integration risk.

steps.description: Identify and assess behaviors that arise from constituent system interactions but are not designed into any single system.

inputs.name: interface-catalog
inputs.desc: Complete interface documentation

inputs.name: mission-objectives
inputs.desc: Intended SoS capabilities

outputs.name: emergent-behavior-catalog
outputs.desc: List of identified emergent behaviors with classification (desired, tolerable, undesirable)

outputs.name: interaction-risk-register
outputs.desc: Risk entries for undesirable emergent behaviors with likelihood and consequence

process: For each pair of interacting systems, ask: what happens if system A sends data that system B interprets differently than intended? Enumerate misinterpretation scenarios from type mismatch, unit mismatch, timing mismatch, and version skew.

Trace feedback loops across three or more systems. A sends to B, B responds to C, C feeds back to A. Identify whether the loop is stabilizing (negative feedback) or amplifying (positive feedback). Amplifying loops produce undesirable emergent behavior unless bounded.

For each identified emergent behavior, classify as: desired (the behavior the SoS exists to produce), tolerable (unintended but harmless), or undesirable (undermines a mission objective or creates a safety hazard).
For undesirable behaviors, estimate likelihood from interface maturity and operational frequency, and consequence from the mission capability affected. Enter into the risk register.

steps.description: Plan how SoS capabilities evolve as constituent systems upgrade independently, including backward compatibility strategy and capability gap closure.

inputs.name: emergent-behavior-catalog
inputs.desc: Known emergent behaviors to preserve or prevent

inputs.name: icd-gap-list
inputs.desc: Interface gaps requiring closure

inputs.name: constituent-profiles
inputs.desc: System evolution schedules and authority

outputs.name: capability-evolution-roadmap
outputs.desc: Phased plan for SoS capability delivery tied to constituent system upgrade schedules

outputs.name: backward-compatibility-requirements
outputs.desc: Interface versioning and backward compatibility rules per interface

process: Collect each constituent system's planned upgrade schedule from its owner. Map capabilities gained and lost at each upgrade milestone.

Identify capability gaps: mission objectives that no current or planned constituent configuration delivers. For each gap, determine whether a new constituent, a new interface, or a modification to an existing constituent closes it.

Define backward compatibility rules for each interface: mandatory backward compatibility window (e.g., must support N-1 version for 12 months), negotiation mechanism (version handshake at session start), and deprecation process.

Build the roadmap as a timeline with swim lanes per constituent. Mark integration milestones where two or more systems must coordinate their upgrades. Flag single-point-of-failure upgrades where one system's delay blocks the entire SoS.

description: Execute model-based systems engineering using SysML: build the model structure, derive functional architecture from use cases, allocate to physical components, and run parametric trade studies.

steps.description: Establish the SysML model structure: package hierarchy, diagram plan, and stereotype/profile definitions for the project.

inputs.name: system-scope
inputs.desc: Boundary of the system being modeled, including external actors and interfaces

inputs.name: stakeholder-concerns
inputs.desc: Key questions each stakeholder group needs the model to answer

outputs.name: model-package-structure
outputs.desc: Hierarchical package tree (requirements, structure, behavior, parametric, analysis) with ownership and access rules

outputs.name: diagram-plan
outputs.desc: List of planned diagrams by type (BDD, IBD, act, sd, stm, par, req) with purpose and owner

process: Define the top-level package structure: Requirements (organized by stakeholder), Structure (BDD hierarchy from system to component), Behavior (activity diagrams for operational scenarios, state machines for modes), Parametric (constraint blocks for physics and trade studies), Analysis (viewpoints for specific stakeholder concerns).

For each stakeholder concern, identify which diagram types answer it. A reliability engineer needs parametric diagrams linking failure rates; a software architect needs IBDs showing data flow. Map concerns to diagrams.

Define stereotypes needed beyond base SysML. Common additions: environment block (external system not under design authority), interface block (reified interface), constraint (physics equation), test case (linked to requirement via verify relationship).

Set model governance rules: naming convention (camelCase for properties, PascalCase for blocks), change control (who can modify which packages), review gates (model reviews at SRR, PDR, CDR milestones).

steps.description: Derive the functional architecture from operational scenarios using activity diagrams, then decompose into a function hierarchy.

inputs.name: model-package-structure
inputs.desc: Established SysML model with package hierarchy

inputs.name: operational-scenarios
inputs.desc: Use cases or operational scenarios the system must support

outputs.name: functional-architecture
outputs.desc: Hierarchy of system functions with input/output flows, organized by operational mode

outputs.name: function-to-requirement-trace
outputs.desc: Traceability from each function to the requirements it satisfies

process: For each operational scenario, build an activity diagram showing the sequence of actions the system performs. Use swim lanes for external actors. Identify object flows (data, energy, material) between actions.

Extract the unique actions across all scenarios. These are the system's functions. Group by abstraction level: mission functions (what the system achieves), operational functions (how it achieves them), and implementation functions (mechanism-specific).
Build the function hierarchy as a BDD where the top-level system block is composed of functional blocks. Each functional block has ports typed by the flows it consumes and produces.

Link each function to the requirements it satisfies using SysML satisfy relationships. Functions with no requirement link are either missing requirements (gap) or unnecessary functions (bloat). Flag both.

steps.description: Allocate logical functions to physical components, resolving many-to-many mappings and documenting allocation rationale.

inputs.name: functional-architecture
inputs.desc: Function hierarchy with flows

inputs.name: physical-architecture-candidates
inputs.desc: Candidate physical components and their capabilities

outputs.name: allocation-matrix
outputs.desc: Function-to-component allocation with rationale for each assignment

outputs.name: interface-block-diagrams
outputs.desc: IBDs showing physical component connections with flow types and protocols

process: Build an allocation matrix with functions as rows and physical components as columns. For each cell, mark allocated, partially allocated, or not allocated. A function split across multiple components requires an interface between them.

For each allocation decision, record the rationale: why this function belongs on this component. Common reasons: processing capacity, physical proximity to sensors/actuators, safety isolation, reuse of existing capability.
For functions allocated across multiple components, define the interface: data exchanged, protocol, latency requirement, and failure mode if the interface breaks.

Build IBDs showing the physical architecture with internal block structure. Ports represent physical interfaces (connectors, buses, wireless links). Flows through ports are typed by the data/energy/material they carry.

steps.description: Use SysML parametric diagrams to run quantitative trade studies, linking design parameters to constraint equations and evaluation criteria.

inputs.name: allocation-matrix
inputs.desc: Function-to-component allocation

inputs.name: trade-study-criteria
inputs.desc: Evaluation criteria with weights for comparing design alternatives

outputs.name: trade-study-results
outputs.desc: Scored alternatives with sensitivity analysis showing which parameters drive the decision

outputs.name: parametric-model
outputs.desc: Constraint blocks linking design parameters to performance metrics through physics equations

process: Define constraint blocks for each physics relationship: mass = sum of component masses, power = sum of component power draws, latency = sum along critical path, reliability = product of component reliabilities (series) or 1 - product of unreliabilities (parallel).

Create a parametric diagram linking design parameters (component choices, material properties, interface bandwidths) through constraint blocks to evaluation criteria (mass, cost, power, reliability, latency).
For each design alternative, set the parameter values and evaluate the constraint network. Record the score per criterion. Apply weights to get an overall score.

Run sensitivity analysis: vary each parameter by +/- 10% and record the change in overall score. Parameters with high sensitivity are the design drivers. If the decision changes within the uncertainty range of a high-sensitivity parameter, the decision is not well-supported and requires more data.

description: Execute deep requirements engineering: elicit stakeholder needs, transform into structured requirements, decompose across levels, build full traceability, and manage change impact.

steps.description: Systematically identify and document stakeholder needs through interviews, observation, prototyping, and CONOPS analysis.

inputs.name: stakeholder-register
inputs.desc: List of stakeholder groups with their roles and authority

inputs.name: system-context
inputs.desc: Operational environment and mission description

outputs.name: needs-register
outputs.desc: Structured list of stakeholder needs with source, priority, and acceptance criteria

outputs.name: conops-document
outputs.desc: Concept of operations describing how the system will be used in its operational environment

process: For each stakeholder group, select the elicitation technique by stakeholder type: end users respond best to observation and prototyping (they show needs they cannot articulate), domain experts to structured interviews (they can articulate constraints), acquirers to CONOPS review (they care about operational fit).

Conduct elicitation sessions. For interviews, use open questions first (what problems do you face?), then probing questions (what happens when X fails?), then confirming questions (so the need is Y, correct?). Record verbatim statements.

Transform raw statements into structured needs: each need has a unique ID, source stakeholder, verbatim statement, interpreted need (rewritten for clarity), priority (must/should/could from MoSCoW), and acceptance criteria (how the stakeholder will judge satisfaction).

Build the CONOPS by sequencing needs into operational scenarios: normal operation, degraded modes, maintenance, startup, shutdown, emergency. Identify needs that conflict between stakeholders and flag for resolution.

steps.description: Transform stakeholder needs into structured, verifiable requirements with shall statements, performance parameters, and verification methods.

inputs.name: needs-register
inputs.desc: Structured stakeholder needs

inputs.name: conops-document
inputs.desc: Operational concept

outputs.name: requirements-set
outputs.desc: Structured requirements with ID, shall statement, rationale, verification method, and parent need trace

outputs.name: requirement-quality-report
outputs.desc: Quality metrics: ambiguity count, testability score, completeness coverage

process: For each need, write one or more shall statements following the pattern: [System/Subsystem] shall [verb] [measurable performance] [under stated conditions]. Every requirement must have a numerical threshold or an unambiguous pass/fail criterion.

For each requirement, assign a verification method: Analysis (calculation or simulation proves compliance), Demonstration (operate the system and observe), Inspection (examine drawings or code), Test (measure performance against threshold). If no method works, the requirement is not verifiable and must be rewritten.
Run ambiguity checks: search for words like 'appropriate', 'sufficient', 'timely', 'user-friendly', 'fast', 'reliable'. Each is ambiguous without a quantified threshold. Replace or define.

Compute quality metrics: completeness = fraction of needs with at least one derived requirement, ambiguity count = flagged words remaining, testability = fraction with assigned verification method, volatility = change rate per review cycle.

steps.description: Decompose system-level requirements to subsystem and component levels, maintaining parent-child traceability and identifying derived requirements.

inputs.name: requirements-set
inputs.desc: System-level requirements

inputs.name: architecture-description
inputs.desc: System architecture showing subsystems and components

outputs.name: decomposed-requirements
outputs.desc: Multi-level requirement tree from system through subsystem to component

outputs.name: derived-requirements-register
outputs.desc: Requirements that exist only because of design decisions, not directly traceable to stakeholder needs

process: For each system requirement, identify which subsystem(s) it applies to based on the architecture allocation. A requirement allocated to a single subsystem flows down directly. A requirement spanning multiple subsystems decomposes into coordinated sub-requirements.

For performance requirements spanning subsystems, apply budgeting: the system-level budget distributes across subsystems. Example: system latency of 100ms with three serial subsystems might allocate 30ms, 40ms, 30ms based on feasibility. Document the allocation rationale.

Identify derived requirements: requirements that arise from the design solution rather than from stakeholder needs. These include interface requirements between subsystems, environmental requirements from physical placement, and standards compliance requirements from the chosen technology. Tag each as derived and link to the design decision that created it.

Build the traceability matrix: rows are component requirements, columns are system requirements. Every component requirement must trace upward. System requirements with no downward trace are unallocated (gap). Component requirements with no upward trace are either derived (tag them) or orphaned (investigate).

steps.description: Analyze the impact of a proposed requirements change across the requirement hierarchy, design, verification, and schedule.

inputs.name: decomposed-requirements
inputs.desc: Full requirement hierarchy with traces

inputs.name: proposed-change
inputs.desc: The requirement change being evaluated: what changes and why

outputs.name: impact-assessment
outputs.desc: Affected requirements, design elements, test cases, and schedule items with severity and cost estimate

outputs.name: change-recommendation
outputs.desc: Accept, reject, or modify recommendation with rationale

process: Identify the directly changed requirement and trace downward: all child requirements that derive from it are potentially impacted. Also trace laterally: requirements that share an interface or a budget with the changed requirement may need adjustment.

For each impacted requirement, assess the design impact: does the current design still satisfy the modified requirement? If not, what design changes are needed? Estimate the effort for each design change.
For each impacted requirement, assess the verification impact: do existing test cases still verify the modified requirement? New test cases needed? Test infrastructure changes? Regression scope?

Aggregate cost, schedule, and risk impacts. Provide a recommendation: accept if the benefits exceed the impacts, reject if impacts are disproportionate, or modify the change to reduce impact while preserving the intent.

description: Execute deep reliability engineering: predict reliability, perform FMEA and fault tree analysis, model reliability architectures, and plan accelerated life testing.

steps.description: Predict system and component reliability using parts stress analysis, handbook methods, and physics-of-failure models.

inputs.name: bill-of-materials
inputs.desc: Component list with part numbers, types, quantities, and stress conditions

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Temperature profile, humidity, vibration, duty cycle

outputs.name: reliability-prediction-report
outputs.desc: Failure rate per component and system MTBF/MTTF with confidence intervals

outputs.name: reliability-drivers-list
outputs.desc: Top 10 components by failure rate contribution (Pareto of unreliability)

process: For each component, determine the base failure rate from the applicable handbook (MIL-HDBK-217F for military, Telcordia SR-332 for telecom, SN 29500 for automotive). Apply stress derating factors: temperature (Arrhenius), voltage stress ratio, current stress ratio.

Calculate the component failure rate: lambda_component = lambda_base * pi_T * pi_V * pi_S * pi_E (temperature, voltage, stress, environment factors). Sum component failure rates for series systems: lambda_system = sum of lambda_component.

Compute system MTBF = 1 / lambda_system for exponential (constant failure rate) assumption. For components with wearout (mechanical, electrolytic capacitors), use Weibull with shape parameter beta > 1.

Build the Pareto chart of failure rate contribution. The top contributors are the reliability drivers. For each driver, assess whether derating, redundancy, or component upgrade reduces the contribution.

steps.description: Execute Failure Mode, Effects, and Criticality Analysis systematically from component through system level.

inputs.name: reliability-prediction-report
inputs.desc: Component failure rates

inputs.name: system-functional-diagram
inputs.desc: Block diagram showing functional flow between components

outputs.name: fmea-worksheet
outputs.desc: Complete FMEA with failure modes, effects, severity/occurrence/detection scores, and RPN

outputs.name: critical-items-list
outputs.desc: Items with RPN above threshold or severity >= 9 regardless of RPN

process: For each component in the functional diagram, enumerate failure modes: open, short, degraded, intermittent, out-of-tolerance, no output, erroneous output. Use component type failure mode distributions from FMECA handbooks.

For each failure mode, trace the effect through the functional chain: local effect (what happens at the component), next-higher effect (what the subsystem experiences), end effect (what the user/mission experiences). The end effect determines severity.

Score severity (1-10 by effect on safety and mission), occurrence (1-10 from failure rate and operating hours), and detection (1-10 by how likely current controls catch the failure before it reaches the end effect). RPN = severity * occurrence * detection.

Rank by RPN. For items above the threshold (typically RPN > 100 or severity >= 9), define corrective actions: design change, added redundancy, improved detection, or operational procedure. Recalculate RPN after corrective action to verify improvement.

steps.description: Build and analyze fault trees: define the top event, construct the tree, compute cut sets, and assess importance measures.

inputs.name: critical-items-list
inputs.desc: Critical failure modes from FMEA

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: Architecture showing redundancy and fault tolerance features

outputs.name: fault-tree-model
outputs.desc: Complete fault tree with top event, intermediate events, basic events, and gate logic

outputs.name: cut-set-analysis
outputs.desc: Minimal cut sets ranked by probability, importance measures (Birnbaum, Fussell-Vesely, RAW, RRW) per basic event

process: Define the top event precisely: 'Loss of system function X during operational phase Y.' Ambiguous top events produce ambiguous trees. The top event must be observable and unambiguous.

Decompose top-down using AND/OR gates. An OR gate means any input causes the output (series reliability). An AND gate means all inputs must occur (parallel/redundant). Continue decomposition until reaching basic events (component failures with known rates).

Compute minimal cut sets: the smallest combinations of basic events that cause the top event. Single-point cut sets (order 1) are the most critical because one failure causes system failure. Order-2 cut sets require two simultaneous failures.

Calculate importance measures: Birnbaum importance = change in top event probability when basic event probability changes from 0 to 1. Fussell-Vesely = fraction of top event probability involving this basic event. Risk Achievement Worth = how much top event probability increases if basic event is certain to fail. Use these to prioritize design improvements.

steps.description: Design accelerated life tests to estimate product reliability in compressed time using physics-based acceleration models.

inputs.name: fault-tree-model
inputs.desc: Identified failure mechanisms and critical components

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Normal use conditions and stress profiles

outputs.name: alt-test-plan
outputs.desc: Test plan with stress levels, sample sizes, duration, acceleration factors, and analysis method

outputs.name: weibull-analysis-template
outputs.desc: Template for Weibull parameter estimation from test data with confidence bounds

process: Identify the dominant failure mechanism for each critical component. Mechanisms determine the acceleration model: Arrhenius for temperature (activation energy Ea), Coffin-Manson for thermal cycling (exponent c, typically 2-3), inverse power for voltage/vibration (exponent n).

Select stress levels. Use at least three levels above normal operating stress. The highest level must accelerate failure without changing the failure mechanism (no new failure modes). Calculate the acceleration factor at each level: AF = exp[(Ea/k)(1/T_use - 1/T_test)] for Arrhenius.

Determine sample size from the required confidence and the number of failures needed for Weibull parameter estimation. For shape parameter beta: 20+ failures give stable estimates. Smaller samples require maximum likelihood estimation with bias correction.

Plan the analysis: fit Weibull distribution to failure times at each stress level. Estimate shape parameter beta (constant across stress levels if the mechanism is the same) and scale parameter eta at each level. Extrapolate eta to use conditions via the acceleration model. Compute B10 life (time to 10% failure) at use conditions with confidence bounds.

description: Execute deep safety engineering: identify hazards using STPA, determine safety integrity levels, design safety functions, analyze common cause failures, and build a safety case.

steps.description: Perform Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis to identify hazards through unsafe control actions and loss scenarios in the control structure.

inputs.name: system-control-structure
inputs.desc: Control structure diagram showing controllers, controlled processes, actuators, sensors, and feedback loops

inputs.name: system-losses
inputs.desc: Unacceptable losses (loss of life, environmental damage, mission failure) the analysis must prevent

outputs.name: unsafe-control-action-table
outputs.desc: UCAs classified by type: not provided, provided incorrectly, wrong timing, stopped too soon

outputs.name: loss-scenario-register
outputs.desc: Causal scenarios for each UCA with contributing factors at controller, actuator, sensor, and process levels

process: Define system-level losses (L1, L2, ...) and trace to system-level hazards (H1, H2, ...): system states that, combined with worst-case environment, lead to a loss. Each hazard must name the system state and the environmental condition.

For each controller in the control structure, enumerate control actions. For each control action, analyze four types of unsafe control action: (1) not provided when needed, (2) provided when not needed, (3) provided too early/too late/wrong order, (4) stopped too soon or applied too long. Link each UCA to the hazard it causes.

For each UCA, identify loss scenarios: what causes the controller to issue the UCA? Analyze at four levels: controller (incorrect process model, flawed algorithm), actuator (fails to execute, executes differently), sensor (provides incorrect feedback), and controlled process (state evolves unexpectedly).

For each loss scenario, identify the causal factor and determine whether a safety constraint (design requirement) can eliminate it. Safety constraints are the output: they become safety requirements in the requirements baseline.

steps.description: Determine the required safety integrity level (SIL per IEC 61508, ASIL per ISO 26262, or DAL per DO-178C) for each safety function.

inputs.name: unsafe-control-action-table
inputs.desc: UCAs with linked hazards

inputs.name: loss-scenario-register
inputs.desc: Causal scenarios with severity estimates

outputs.name: sil-allocation-table
outputs.desc: Safety integrity level per safety function with determination rationale

outputs.name: target-failure-measures
outputs.desc: PFDavg for low-demand functions, PFH for high-demand/continuous, with target values per SIL

process: For IEC 61508: use risk graph method or risk matrix. Inputs: consequence severity (C1-C4), frequency of exposure (F1-F2), probability of avoidance (P1-P2), demand rate (W1-W3). The intersection determines SIL 1-4.
For ISO 26262: compute ASIL from severity (S0-S3), exposure probability (E0-E4), and controllability (C0-C3). ASIL = S x E x C lookup. ASIL D is the highest, QM is the lowest (no safety requirement).
For each SIL/ASIL, look up the target failure measure. IEC 61508 low-demand: PFDavg (SIL 1 = 0.01-0.1, SIL 2 = 0.001-0.01, SIL 3 = 0.0001-0.001, SIL 4 = 0.00001-0.0001). High-demand/continuous: PFH.

Allocate SIL to safety functions. If a single safety function addresses multiple hazards, it must meet the highest SIL. If multiple independent safety functions protect against the same hazard, their combined SIL may exceed the individual SILs by one level (SIL claim limit).

steps.description: Design safety functions meeting the allocated SIL, including sensor, logic, and actuator selection with architectural constraints.

inputs.name: sil-allocation-table
inputs.desc: SIL per safety function

inputs.name: target-failure-measures
inputs.desc: PFDavg or PFH targets

outputs.name: safety-function-architecture
outputs.desc: Sensor-logic-actuator architecture per safety function with hardware fault tolerance and safe failure fraction

outputs.name: pfd-calculation
outputs.desc: Calculated PFDavg or PFH per safety function demonstrating SIL compliance

process: For each safety function, select the architecture by SIL: SIL 1 may use 1oo1 (single channel), SIL 2 typically 1oo1D (single with diagnostics) or 1oo2, SIL 3 requires 1oo2D or 2oo3, SIL 4 requires 2oo3 or higher with separation. The architecture must achieve the required hardware fault tolerance (HFT) and safe failure fraction (SFF).

Select sensor, logic solver, and actuator for each channel. Each element has a failure rate (lambda) split into dangerous detected (DD), dangerous undetected (DU), safe detected (SD), and safe undetected (SU). The SFF = (SD + SU + DD) / (SD + SU + DD + DU).

Calculate PFDavg or PFH for the safety function using the Markov model or simplified equations from IEC 61508 Part 6. For 1oo2 architecture: PFDavg = 2 * ((lambda_DU * T_proof)^2) / 3 + lambda_DU * MTTR (with common cause beta factor adjustment).

Verify the calculated PFD/PFH meets the target. If not, improve by: increasing proof test frequency (reduces T_proof), improving diagnostics (moves failures from DU to DD), adding redundancy (adds channels), or selecting higher-reliability components (reduces lambda).

steps.description: Build a structured safety case using Goal Structuring Notation linking claims to evidence through a documented argument.

inputs.name: safety-function-architecture
inputs.desc: Safety function designs with architecture choices

inputs.name: pfd-calculation
inputs.desc: PFD/PFH compliance calculations

outputs.name: safety-case-structure
outputs.desc: GSN diagram with goals, strategies, contexts, solutions (evidence), and assumptions

outputs.name: evidence-gap-register
outputs.desc: Evidence items required but not yet available, with plan to obtain

process: Define the top-level goal: 'System is acceptably safe for operation in [context].' Decompose using strategies: 'Argument over identified hazards' (each hazard gets a sub-goal), 'Argument over safety functions' (each function gets a sub-goal), 'Argument over lifecycle management' (process compliance).

For each hazard sub-goal, the argument links to: hazard analysis evidence (STPA results), risk assessment (SIL determination), mitigation design (safety function architecture), and verification (test results showing the function works as designed).

For each evidence item (solution node in GSN), assess its status: complete (evidence exists and is reviewed), in progress (evidence generation underway), or gap (not yet started). Enter gaps into the evidence gap register with a plan and due date.

Review the safety case for argument defeaters: assumptions that, if violated, break the argument. Each assumption must be stated explicitly. Common implicit assumptions: failure independence (requires common cause analysis), constant failure rate (requires wearout analysis), representative test conditions (requires test coverage argument).

description: Plan and execute system verification and validation: derive test cases from requirements, design the V&V strategy, build test environments, and package evidence for certification.

steps.description: Design the V&V strategy mapping each requirement to a verification method and integrating unit, integration, system, and acceptance test levels.

inputs.name: requirements-baseline
inputs.desc: Complete requirements set with verification method assigned per requirement

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: Architecture decomposition showing test boundaries

outputs.name: vv-strategy-document
outputs.desc: V&V plan with test levels, entry/exit criteria, test environment needs, and schedule

outputs.name: verification-cross-reference-matrix
outputs.desc: Requirement-to-test-case mapping showing complete coverage

process: Map each requirement to the V-model level where it will be verified: component requirements at unit test, interface requirements at integration test, system requirements at system test, stakeholder needs at acceptance test. A requirement may be partially verified at multiple levels.

For each test level, define entry criteria (what must be complete before testing begins), exit criteria (what constitutes test completion), suspension criteria (when to stop testing), and resumption criteria (when to restart).

Identify test environment needs per level: unit test may need stubs and drivers, integration test may need hardware-in-the-loop, system test may need the operational environment or a high-fidelity simulation, acceptance test needs the actual operational environment.

Build the verification cross-reference matrix (VCRM): rows are requirements, columns are test cases. Every requirement must have at least one test case. Test cases with no linked requirement are either testing derived requirements (link them) or are redundant.

steps.description: Derive test cases systematically from requirements using equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and decision table techniques.

inputs.name: vv-strategy-document
inputs.desc: V&V plan identifying which requirements are verified by test

inputs.name: requirements-baseline
inputs.desc: Requirements with numerical thresholds and conditions

outputs.name: test-case-suite
outputs.desc: Complete test case set with preconditions, steps, expected results, and pass/fail criteria

outputs.name: test-coverage-analysis
outputs.desc: Coverage metrics: requirement coverage, boundary coverage, decision coverage

process: For each testable requirement, identify the input domain (all valid and invalid input combinations) and partition into equivalence classes: ranges of inputs that the system should handle identically. Select one representative test case per equivalence class.

For numerical requirements, apply boundary value analysis: test at the boundary value, one increment below, and one increment above. For a requirement 'system shall respond within 100ms', test at 99ms (pass), 100ms (pass), and 101ms (fail).

For requirements with multiple conditions, build a decision table: columns are condition combinations, rows are expected actions. Each column becomes a test case. Reduce the table by identifying 'don't care' conditions that do not affect the outcome.

Compute coverage metrics: requirement coverage = requirements with at least one test case / total requirements. For structural coverage (if code is available): statement coverage, branch coverage, MC/DC for safety-critical software per DO-178C.

steps.description: Design and specify test environments for each V&V level, including hardware-in-the-loop, software-in-the-loop, and digital twin configurations.

inputs.name: test-case-suite
inputs.desc: Test cases requiring specific environments

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: Architecture showing what can be simulated vs what must be real hardware

outputs.name: test-environment-specs
outputs.desc: Per-level environment specifications: hardware, software, simulation models, interfaces, and calibration requirements

outputs.name: test-environment-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Risks from environment fidelity gaps and mitigation through test at higher levels

process: For each test level, determine the mix of real hardware and simulation. Unit test: all simulation except the unit under test. Integration test: real components at the integration boundary, simulated components elsewhere. System test: all real components, simulated operational environment. Acceptance test: all real.

For simulated components, specify fidelity requirements: functional fidelity (produces correct outputs for given inputs), timing fidelity (responds within realistic latency), fault injection capability (can simulate failure modes). Lower fidelity costs less but risks missing integration issues.

Design the hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) configuration for integration and system test: real controller hardware, simulated plant, real or simulated sensors/actuators, real communication buses. Specify the real-time simulation platform (dSPACE, NI, Speedgoat) and the plant model fidelity.

Assess environment risk: for each test case, what defects could be missed because the environment does not perfectly replicate the operational environment? Mitigate by: testing the high-risk cases at the next level with higher fidelity, or by analysis showing the simulation error is within acceptable bounds.

steps.description: Package V&V evidence into a certification-ready data package meeting the applicable standard's documentation requirements.

inputs.name: test-case-suite
inputs.desc: Executed test cases with results

inputs.name: test-coverage-analysis
inputs.desc: Coverage metrics

inputs.name: test-environment-specs
inputs.desc: Environment descriptions and calibration records

outputs.name: certification-data-package
outputs.desc: Organized evidence package: test procedures, results, coverage analysis, environment qualification, traceability, and compliance matrix

outputs.name: open-problem-report-list
outputs.desc: Unresolved test failures with disposition (waiver, retest, design change)

process: Organize evidence by the certification standard's structure. DO-178C: Plans, Standards, Software Requirements, Design, Source Code, Test Cases/Procedures/Results, Configuration Index, Quality Assurance Records, Accomplishment Summary. IEC 61508: Safety Plan, Specification, Design, V&V Plan, V&V Report, Safety Manual.

For each test case, verify the evidence chain: test procedure (what was done) -> test results (what was observed) -> pass/fail judgment (against expected results) -> requirement trace (which requirement is verified). Missing links break the evidence chain.

For unresolved test failures, document the disposition: design change (fix the defect and retest), waiver (accept the deviation with justification), retest (suspected false failure, test again), or deferral (accept for initial certification with plan to fix). Each disposition requires approval authority signature.

Build the compliance matrix: rows are standard requirements (e.g., DO-178C Table A-1 through A-10), columns are evidence items. Every standard requirement must have at least one evidence item. Empty cells are compliance gaps that block certification.

description: Execute a rigorous trade study: define criteria with AHP weighting, generate alternatives through morphological analysis, score with utility functions, and validate with sensitivity analysis.

steps.description: Define and weight decision criteria using the Analytic Hierarchy Process with consistency validation.

inputs.name: decision-context
inputs.desc: What is being decided, why, and who the decision makers are

inputs.name: candidate-criteria
inputs.desc: Initial list of evaluation criteria from stakeholders

outputs.name: weighted-criteria
outputs.desc: Criteria with AHP-derived weights, consistency ratio, and stakeholder agreement status

outputs.name: criteria-hierarchy
outputs.desc: If criteria have sub-criteria, the full hierarchy with weights at each level

process: Screen candidate criteria: remove duplicates, merge overlapping criteria, ensure each criterion is independent (changing one does not mechanically change another). A good trade study uses 5-9 criteria; more than 9 overwhelms the pairwise comparison.

Build the pairwise comparison matrix. For each pair of criteria, the decision maker rates relative importance on the Saaty scale: 1 = equal, 3 = moderate, 5 = strong, 7 = very strong, 9 = extreme. The matrix is reciprocal: if A vs B = 5, then B vs A = 1/5.

Compute the priority vector (weights) by normalizing the eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Calculate the consistency ratio: CR = CI / RI where CI = (lambda_max - n) / (n - 1) and RI is the random index for matrix size n. CR must be < 0.10 or the comparisons are inconsistent and must be revised.

If multiple decision makers participate, aggregate their individual pairwise matrices using the geometric mean method (row-by-row geometric mean across participants). Recompute weights and consistency from the aggregated matrix.

steps.description: Generate design alternatives systematically using morphological analysis, exploring the full parameter space and eliminating infeasible combinations.

inputs.name: design-parameters
inputs.desc: Independent design dimensions (e.g., power source, material, architecture type, cooling method)

inputs.name: constraints
inputs.desc: Hard constraints that eliminate certain parameter combinations

outputs.name: morphological-matrix
outputs.desc: Parameter matrix with options per parameter

outputs.name: feasible-alternatives
outputs.desc: Reduced set of alternatives after cross-consistency assessment eliminates infeasible combinations

process: Build the morphological matrix: rows are design parameters (independent dimensions of the solution space), columns are the possible options for each parameter. The total solution space is the product of options per parameter.

Perform cross-consistency assessment: for each pair of parameters, check whether each option combination is compatible. Mark incompatible pairs. Example: if power source = solar and location = underground, the combination is infeasible.
Eliminate all alternatives containing at least one infeasible pair. The remaining alternatives are the feasible set. Typically this reduces the solution space by 90% or more.

From the feasible set, select 3-7 representative alternatives for detailed evaluation. Include at least one low-risk/conventional option, one high-performance option, and one cost-optimized option. Avoid evaluating only similar alternatives.

steps.description: Score alternatives against weighted criteria using utility functions that convert raw performance into normalized scores.

inputs.name: weighted-criteria
inputs.desc: Criteria with AHP-derived weights

inputs.name: feasible-alternatives
inputs.desc: Alternatives to evaluate

inputs.name: performance-data
inputs.desc: Raw performance estimates per alternative per criterion

outputs.name: scored-alternatives
outputs.desc: Alternatives ranked by weighted utility score

outputs.name: scoring-rationale
outputs.desc: Per-cell documentation of how raw performance was converted to utility and the data source

process: For each criterion, define the utility function that maps raw performance to a 0-1 scale. Linear: utility = (value - worst) / (best - worst). Threshold: utility = 0 below threshold, 1 above. Diminishing returns: utility = 1 - exp(-k * value). The function shape must match how stakeholders value improvement.

For each alternative-criterion cell, estimate the raw performance. Document the source: analysis, simulation, vendor data, expert judgment, or historical data from similar systems. Assign a confidence level (high, medium, low) to each estimate.
Convert raw performance to utility using the defined function. Multiply utility by criterion weight. Sum weighted utilities across criteria to get the total score per alternative.

Rank alternatives by total score. Identify the margin between the top two alternatives. If the margin is smaller than the uncertainty in the estimates, the decision is not statistically significant and requires either better data or additional discriminating criteria.

steps.description: Validate the trade study result through sensitivity analysis on weights and performance estimates to identify conditions under which the decision changes.

inputs.name: scored-alternatives
inputs.desc: Ranked alternatives with weighted scores

inputs.name: weighted-criteria
inputs.desc: Criteria weights

inputs.name: performance-data
inputs.desc: Raw performance estimates with confidence levels

outputs.name: sensitivity-report
outputs.desc: Tornado diagram, weight sensitivity ranges, Monte Carlo results showing decision stability

outputs.name: decision-recommendation
outputs.desc: Final recommendation with confidence level and conditions for revisiting

process: One-at-a-time weight sensitivity: for each criterion, increase its weight by 20% (scaling others proportionally) and check if the ranking changes. The criteria where a 20% increase changes the winner are the decision-sensitive criteria. Present as a tornado diagram.

Performance estimate sensitivity: for each low-confidence estimate, vary it by the uncertainty range and check if the ranking changes. If a single estimate change flips the decision, that estimate needs refinement before the decision is defensible.

Monte Carlo simulation: treat each performance estimate as a distribution (uniform for low confidence, triangular for medium, normal for high). Sample 10,000 combinations and record which alternative wins each trial. The win percentage is the decision confidence.

Write the recommendation: state the winning alternative, the confidence level from Monte Carlo, the conditions under which the decision should be revisited (which criteria weights or performance values changing would flip it), and any dissenting opinions from the decision team.

description: Plan and execute systems integration: assess interface maturity, sequence integration builds, design test environments, and resolve integration anomalies.

steps.description: Plan the integration sequence by analyzing interface dependencies and defining incremental build milestones.

inputs.name: interface-catalog
inputs.desc: All system interfaces with maturity scores and criticality

inputs.name: component-delivery-schedule
inputs.desc: When each component is available for integration

outputs.name: integration-sequence
outputs.desc: Ordered sequence of integration builds with components added at each build and interfaces exercised

outputs.name: integration-risk-register
outputs.desc: Risks per build: immature interfaces, component delays, test coverage gaps

process: Build the interface dependency graph: nodes are components, edges are interfaces. Identify the critical path through the graph: the longest chain of dependent integrations that determines the minimum integration duration.

Define integration builds. Each build adds one or more components to the integrated set. Sequence builds so that: (1) components with the most interfaces are integrated first (they drive the most defect discovery), (2) high-risk interfaces are exercised early (fail fast), (3) component availability is respected.

For each build, define the scope: which interfaces are exercised for the first time, which are regression-tested, what test environment configuration is needed. Assign a build coordinator responsible for the build's entry/exit criteria.

Identify integration risks: interfaces with maturity below 3 (poorly documented), components expected to arrive late, interfaces that cross organizational boundaries (ICD disagreements likely). For each risk, define a mitigation: early interface simulation, schedule buffer, interface working group.

steps.description: Verify interfaces at each integration build: protocol conformance, data format correctness, timing compliance, and error handling.

inputs.name: integration-sequence
inputs.desc: Current build scope and interfaces to verify

inputs.name: interface-catalog
inputs.desc: ICD specifications for each interface

outputs.name: interface-test-results
outputs.desc: Pass/fail per interface per test case with failure details

outputs.name: interface-defect-log
outputs.desc: Defects found with classification: ICD error, implementation error, environment error

process: For each interface in the current build, execute protocol conformance tests: does each side follow the specified handshake, message format, and error codes? Use a protocol analyzer or bus monitor to capture actual traffic and compare to the ICD.

Test data format correctness: send valid data and verify correct interpretation. Send boundary values and verify correct handling. Send invalid data and verify the receiver rejects it gracefully (does not crash, does not silently accept corrupt data).
Test timing: measure actual latency and compare to the ICD specification. Inject delays to verify timeout and retry behavior. Test under load to verify timing holds when the bus is busy.

Classify each defect: ICD error (the specification is wrong or ambiguous, both sides implemented correctly but incompatibly), implementation error (one side does not follow the ICD), or environment error (the test setup caused the failure, not the system under test). ICD errors require ICD change and bilateral agreement.

steps.description: Resolve integration anomalies through structured triage, root cause analysis, corrective action, and regression verification.

inputs.name: interface-defect-log
inputs.desc: Defects from integration testing

inputs.name: integration-sequence
inputs.desc: Current and upcoming build schedule

outputs.name: corrective-action-register
outputs.desc: Per-defect corrective actions with owner, due date, and verification plan

outputs.name: regression-test-plan
outputs.desc: Tests to re-run after corrective actions to verify the fix and catch regressions

process: Triage each anomaly: severity (blocks integration, degrades performance, cosmetic), reproducibility (always, intermittent, once), and urgency (blocks current build, blocks next build, can defer). Assign priority from the triage.

For each high-priority anomaly, perform root cause analysis. Use the 5-why method or Ishikawa diagram. Common integration root causes: mismatched ICD versions, endianness mismatch, race condition under load, clock drift between systems, configuration error in the test environment.

Define corrective action: what changes, in which component, by whom, by when. For ICD errors, the corrective action is an ICD update followed by implementation changes on both sides. For implementation errors, the corrective action is a component fix followed by unit retest before re-integration.

Define regression scope: which previously passing tests must re-run after the fix? At minimum, re-run all tests for the modified interface. If the fix changes a shared component, re-run all interfaces involving that component.

description: Build and operate a digital twin: select the physics model, integrate sensor data, calibrate from operation, and apply for predictive maintenance and scenario analysis.

steps.description: Select the appropriate physics model fidelity for the digital twin based on the use case, available data, and computational constraints.

inputs.name: twin-use-cases
inputs.desc: What the digital twin must answer: condition monitoring, predictive maintenance, design optimization, scenario analysis

inputs.name: available-sensor-data
inputs.desc: Sensors installed, their measurement types, sample rates, and data quality

outputs.name: model-selection-rationale
outputs.desc: Selected model type with justification against alternatives

outputs.name: model-specification
outputs.desc: Model inputs, outputs, state variables, parameters, assumptions, and validity envelope

process: Match model fidelity to use case: condition monitoring needs a simple threshold or regression model, predictive maintenance needs a physics-of-degradation model (crack growth, wear, corrosion), design optimization needs a high-fidelity FEA/CFD model or surrogate, scenario analysis needs a real-time capable model.

Assess available data against model needs. A physics model requires boundary conditions (loads, temperatures, pressures) that sensors must provide. If key boundary conditions are not measured, either add sensors, estimate from related measurements, or reduce model fidelity to match available data.

Consider computational constraints: high-fidelity FEA/CFD may take hours per simulation, making it unsuitable for real-time operation. Options: reduced-order model (POD, DMD), surrogate model (Gaussian process, neural network trained on full model), or physics-informed neural network (PINN).

Document the model validity envelope: the range of operating conditions where the model's predictions are trustworthy. Outside this envelope, the twin should flag low confidence rather than extrapolate.

steps.description: Integrate real-time sensor data into the digital twin to update its state estimate, using Kalman filtering or particle filtering.

inputs.name: model-specification
inputs.desc: Twin physics model with state variables and parameters

inputs.name: available-sensor-data
inputs.desc: Real-time sensor streams with noise characteristics

outputs.name: assimilation-architecture
outputs.desc: Data flow from sensors through filtering to twin state update, with update frequency and latency

outputs.name: state-estimation-validation
outputs.desc: Validation plan comparing twin state estimates to independent measurements

process: Map sensors to model states. Each sensor measures a function of the model state vector: z = h(x) + noise. The measurement function h maps model states to sensor output. If a state has no sensor mapping, it is observable only through model dynamics.

Select the filtering algorithm. Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for mildly nonlinear systems with Gaussian noise. Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for moderately nonlinear systems. Particle filter for highly nonlinear systems with non-Gaussian noise. EnKF for high-dimensional systems (large state vector).

Tune filter parameters: process noise covariance Q (how much the model state is expected to deviate from predictions between updates) and measurement noise covariance R (sensor noise). Q too small: the filter trusts the model too much and ignores sensor data. R too small: the filter trusts sensors too much and becomes noisy.

Design the validation approach: periodically compare the twin's state estimate to independent measurements not used in the assimilation (holdout sensors or periodic inspections). If the twin diverges beyond an acceptable threshold, trigger recalibration.

steps.description: Calibrate the digital twin's parameters from operational data using Bayesian inference or optimization-based parameter estimation.

inputs.name: assimilation-architecture
inputs.desc: Data flow and filtering setup

inputs.name: operational-data-history
inputs.desc: Historical sensor data with known operating conditions

outputs.name: calibrated-parameters
outputs.desc: Model parameters with uncertainty estimates (posterior distribution or confidence intervals)

outputs.name: calibration-quality-metrics
outputs.desc: Residual analysis, prediction vs measurement correlation, coverage probability

process: Identify calibration parameters: model parameters that cannot be determined from first principles and must be estimated from data. Examples: friction coefficients, heat transfer coefficients, degradation rates. Fix parameters that are known from material data sheets or manufacturer specifications.

Formulate the calibration problem. Optimization approach: minimize sum of squared residuals (prediction - measurement)^2 over the parameter space. Bayesian approach: define prior distributions on parameters, compute the likelihood from residuals, obtain posterior distributions via MCMC or variational inference.

Execute calibration on historical data. Split data into calibration set (70%) and validation set (30%). Fit on calibration set, evaluate on validation set. If validation residuals are significantly larger than calibration residuals, the model is overfitting.

Report calibrated parameters with uncertainty. For optimization: parameter values with confidence intervals from the Hessian at the optimum. For Bayesian: posterior mean and credible intervals. Large uncertainty indicates the data does not constrain that parameter well.

steps.description: Apply the calibrated digital twin for predictive maintenance: estimate remaining useful life from degradation trajectories and optimize maintenance scheduling.

inputs.name: calibrated-parameters
inputs.desc: Model parameters including degradation rates

inputs.name: maintenance-cost-model
inputs.desc: Cost of planned vs unplanned maintenance, downtime cost, spare parts lead time

outputs.name: rul-estimates
outputs.desc: Remaining useful life per monitored component with confidence intervals

outputs.name: maintenance-schedule
outputs.desc: Recommended maintenance actions with timing optimized for cost and risk

process: Run the degradation model forward from the current state (estimated by the twin) to the failure threshold. The time to reach the threshold is the remaining useful life (RUL). Propagate parameter uncertainty through the prediction to get RUL confidence intervals.

For components where the degradation model has multiple possible trajectories (e.g., crack growth depends on future loading), run Monte Carlo simulations with sampled future load profiles to get a RUL distribution.

Optimize maintenance timing using the RUL distribution and cost model. The expected cost is: P(fail before maintenance) * unplanned_cost + P(survive to maintenance) * planned_cost + downtime_cost. Minimize expected cost over the maintenance date.

Generate the maintenance schedule: per component, the recommended action (inspect, replace, overhaul), the recommended date, the confidence level, and the cost-risk trade-off. Flag components where the RUL confidence interval is wide enough that the maintenance timing decision is uncertain.

description: Engineer system resilience: define resilience metrics, model disruption scenarios, design graceful degradation, plan recovery, and test through controlled disruption.

steps.description: Define quantitative resilience metrics covering absorptive capacity, adaptive capacity, and restorative capacity.

inputs.name: system-functions
inputs.desc: List of system functions with their performance metrics

inputs.name: stakeholder-resilience-needs
inputs.desc: What stakeholders consider acceptable degradation and recovery time

outputs.name: resilience-metric-set
outputs.desc: Defined metrics with measurement method, baseline values, and acceptable thresholds

outputs.name: resilience-profile-template
outputs.desc: Template for plotting system performance vs time through disruption-degradation-recovery cycle

process: Define the performance function Q(t): the normalized performance level (0 = total loss, 1 = full nominal) as a function of time. The resilience profile is the shape of Q(t) through a disruption event.

Define absorptive capacity metrics: the minimum performance level Q_min during disruption (how deep the dip is), and the performance drop rate dQ/dt during the disruption onset (how fast performance degrades). A system that degrades slowly absorbs the disruption better.

Define adaptive capacity metrics: the steady-state performance level Q_adapted during sustained disruption (after initial transient but before recovery). This measures whether the system can find a new operating mode that delivers partial capability.

Define restorative capacity metrics: time to recover to 90% of nominal (T_90), and recovery rate dQ/dt during restoration. Also define the resilience integral: the area between the nominal performance line and the actual Q(t) curve, which captures total performance loss over the disruption lifecycle.

steps.description: Model disruption scenarios using threat-vulnerability-consequence analysis and simulate cascading effects across coupled subsystems.

inputs.name: resilience-metric-set
inputs.desc: Metrics to evaluate per scenario

inputs.name: system-architecture
inputs.desc: System structure showing dependencies and coupling between subsystems

outputs.name: disruption-scenario-set
outputs.desc: Defined scenarios with trigger event, affected subsystems, propagation path, and expected performance impact

outputs.name: cascading-failure-analysis
outputs.desc: For each scenario, the cascade sequence showing how failure propagates through dependencies

process: Enumerate threat categories: natural (earthquake, flood, extreme weather), technical (component failure, software defect, power loss), human (operator error, malicious attack, supply chain disruption), organizational (budget cut, personnel turnover, regulatory change).

For each threat, identify the directly affected subsystem (vulnerability) and the immediate performance impact (consequence). Then trace the cascade: if subsystem A fails, which subsystems depend on A? For each dependent subsystem B, what is B's response to A's failure? Does B have fallback? If B fails, trace further.
Model the cascade timing: some cascades propagate in milliseconds (electrical), some in minutes (thermal), some in days (supply chain). The cascade speed determines whether intervention is possible.

For each scenario, simulate (or reason about) the performance profile Q(t): initial performance, disruption onset, minimum performance, adaptation, recovery. Evaluate the resilience metrics defined earlier.

steps.description: Design graceful degradation strategies that preserve essential functions when full performance is impossible.

inputs.name: disruption-scenario-set
inputs.desc: Scenarios showing which subsystems fail

inputs.name: system-functions
inputs.desc: Functions prioritized by criticality

outputs.name: degradation-mode-table
outputs.desc: Per disruption: which functions are maintained, which are shed, and how the transition occurs

outputs.name: mode-transition-logic
outputs.desc: Decision rules for entering and exiting each degradation mode

process: Prioritize system functions into tiers: Tier 1 (safety-critical, never shed), Tier 2 (mission-essential, shed only as last resort), Tier 3 (performance-enhancing, shed first), Tier 4 (convenience, shed immediately under any disruption).

For each disruption scenario, determine which functions can still be provided with the remaining resources. Start by shedding Tier 4, then Tier 3, working upward until the remaining functions fit within available resources. Document the resulting degradation mode.

Design the mode transition: what triggers the transition (detection mechanism), what actions occur during transition (function handoff, load shedding, user notification), how long the transition takes, and what happens if the trigger is a false alarm (reversion mechanism).

For each degradation mode, verify that safety functions (Tier 1) remain available. If a disruption scenario can take out a safety function, the system needs additional redundancy or diversity for that function.

steps.description: Plan and execute resilience testing through controlled disruption injection to validate degradation and recovery behavior.

inputs.name: degradation-mode-table
inputs.desc: Expected behavior per disruption

inputs.name: mode-transition-logic
inputs.desc: Decision rules to verify

outputs.name: resilience-test-plan
outputs.desc: Test cases: inject disruption, measure performance profile, compare to expected degradation and recovery

outputs.name: resilience-test-results
outputs.desc: Measured Q(t) profiles per scenario with pass/fail against resilience metric thresholds

process: Design disruption injection methods for each scenario: hardware fault injection (kill a power supply, disconnect a network cable, inject corrupted sensor data), software fault injection (crash a process, fill a disk, delay a message), and environmental simulation (thermal chamber, vibration table, RF interference).

For each test, define: precondition (system at nominal), injection (specific disruption at specific time), observation (performance metrics sampled at 1Hz or faster during disruption), duration (long enough to observe adaptation and initiate recovery), and cleanup (restore the disrupted element).

Execute tests in order of increasing severity: start with single-point disruptions (one subsystem at a time), then combinations (two simultaneous disruptions), then cascading scenarios (disrupt A and observe whether B fails). For each test, record Q(t) and compare to the expected degradation mode.

Evaluate results against resilience metric thresholds: did Q_min stay above the acceptable minimum? Did T_90 stay below the acceptable recovery time? For failures, trace the root cause: was the degradation mode incorrect (design issue), or was the mode transition too slow (implementation issue)?
